stem: The constellation of symptoms and signs in this patient is most accurately described as:
explanation: This child has a classic cerebellar toxidrome: somnolence, dysarthria, truncal and limb ataxia, nystagmus, and dysmetria with normal strength, tone, reflexes, and MRI. The pattern is best described as a pancerebellar syndrome, often seen with sedative or anticonvulsant ingestion.

optionExplanations.A: Hemiplegia would cause unilateral weakness and upper motor neuron signs, which are not present.
optionExplanations.B: Spastic diplegia is a chronic motor pattern with bilateral leg spasticity, not an acute presentation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: the findings localise to diffuse cerebellar dysfunction affecting gait, speech, coordination, and eye movements.
optionExplanations.D: A spinal cord syndrome would produce weakness, sensory changes, or reflex abnormalities, which are absent.

Instructions

Question 1 & 2 relate to this case

Case 1

A 4 year old is brought into ED as his mother found him to be sleepy and very unsteady on waking up this morning. His parents have been separated for 2 years and he had spent the night before at his father’s house. The boy has not been otherwise unwell and there is no concern about trauma. He is developmentally normal and his growth has been following the 75th centile lines.

On examination weight, head circumference and height are on 75th centiles. His BP is 100/70 and he is afebrile. He does not have a rash. He is difficult to rouse but can answer basic questions. His speech is slurred but you are able to make out that he had some ‘orange lollies’ last night that he found in his dads cupboard. He cannot walk or sit without falling to both sides. He has nystagmus in all directions and slurred speech but the rest of his cranial nerves are normal. He has normal tone, power and reflexes. He is very shaky when trying to get the lid off your pen and cannot replace the lid. He wants to fall asleep. You question his mum about any possible medications that he could have had access to and she has a vague recollection that his father has ‘funny turns’ for which he takes a daily medication but she can’t recall what it’s called.

You do screening blood tests including a full blood count, liver function tests and a blood gas and they are normal. You request an MRI and it too is normal. A urine toxicology screen is still pending.
